title: Running from a fire
translation: If you've decided to take the big step and give your life to the Buddhist path, don't wait to finish the things you can't let go of. Drop them as they are.

"Just let me finish this first." "While I'm at it, I'll sort out that other thing." "People will laugh if I leave this undone." "I'll get everything in order so there's no trouble later." "It's not as if it'll take years. I can wait that long." "I don't want to leave in a mess." Think like that, and the things you can't drop just keep piling up. They never run out, and the day you actually go never comes.
Look at people in general. Even the ones with a bit of sense seem to spend their whole lives on plans like these.

When there's a fire next door, does anyone running from it say "Just a moment"? To save yourself, you don't care how it looks, you leave your things behind, and you run. Does death wait for anyone? It comes faster than fire or flood, and there's no getting away from it. When it comes, can you say that your old parents, your little children, your duty to your lord and the people who were kind to you are too hard to leave, and not leave them?

literal: A person who resolves on the great matter should not carry out his wishes concerning things that weigh on his mind and are hard to give up, but should abandon them just as they are.

'For a while (wait until) this matter is finished; if it's all the same, let me settle that matter; about such-and-such a thing, might people not mock me?; let me arrange things so that there is no trouble in the future; if it were years, that would be one thing, but there won't be much time to wait for that matter; let me make it so that it is not hectic': if one thinks such things,
the things one cannot get away from only pile up more and more, there is no end to the matters, and there will be no day on which one sets out.
Looking at people in general, those of the level that have a little sense all seem to pass their lifetime with such plans.
Does a person fleeing from a nearby fire say 'Just a moment'?
If he is to save himself, he does not consider shame, throws away his wealth too, and escapes.

The coming of impermanence is quicker than the attack of water and fire, and hard to escape, yet at that time, will you not abandon the old parents, the young children, the lord's favour and people's kindness, saying they are hard to abandon?

notes.text: {大事|だいじ}: 'the great matter'. The 1925 edition explains: here, Buddhist practice, that is, leaving the world to become a monk.

notes.quote: さながら捨つべきなり
notes.text: さながら: 'just as it is, all of it'. べし: 'should'. Leave the unfinished things unfinished.

notes.quote: 年ごろもあればこそあれ
notes.text: The 1925 edition explains it: 'if it took years, that would be one thing, but it will only take a short time'. That is the excuse: it won't take long.

notes.quote: このあらましにてぞ一期は過ぐめる
notes.text: あらまし: 'plans, intentions'. {一期|いちご}: a whole lifetime. ぞ … める: めり ('it seems') takes the attributive form. Not only fools live like this, but people with some sense too.
や: a rhetorical question, 'does he say…? (He doesn't.)'. The section turns on this image.

notes.quote: 命は人を待つものかは
notes.text: かは: another rhetorical question. Three in a row close the section: the man at the fire, death, and you.
{水火|すいくわ}: water and fire, that is, flood and fire. The fire next door comes back as a general rule.
'Will you not abandon them?' The answer the text expects is: you will have to. Death will take you away from all of them anyway.
